topic: S3.2 Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
subject: chemistry

items.q: Propan-2-ol has the molecular formula C₃H₈O. Which statement about the formula C₃H₈O is correct?
items.correct: It is both the molecular and the empirical formula of propan-2-ol.
items.misconception: It is the molecular formula only, since an empirical formula is simpler.
items.why: The first examples students meet are chosen to show a difference (C₂H₆ and CH₃, C₆H₁₂O₆ and CH₂O), and the word 'simplest' is read as 'must be simplified'. The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. Divide the subscripts by their highest common factor; if that factor is 1, the ratio is already in its simplest form and the empirical and molecular formulas are identical.
items.specStatementText: Organic compounds can be represented by different types of formulas. These include empirical, molecular, structural (full and condensed), stereochemical and skeletal.
items.random_wrong: It is a condensed structural formula, as it lists every atom present.

items.q: The skeletal formula of a compound is a zig-zag line of five straight segments joined end to end. An –OH group is drawn at the point where the first and second segments meet (the second point from the left-hand end). No other atoms are shown. What is the molecular formula of the compound?
items.correct: C₆H₁₄O
items.misconception: C₅H₁₂O
items.why:
Students carry over the idea that each symbol drawn is an atom, and count the most visible marks, the lines, rather than the points where they meet. Lines are bonds; carbon atoms sit at every end and every bend. A chain of n segments with no branches has n + 1 carbon atoms.

Working: Carbon atoms: 5 segments give 5 + 1 = 6 points, each a carbon atom. Hydrogen atoms (4 bonds per carbon): point 1 CH₃ (3), point 2 CH bonded to OH (1), points 3–5 CH₂ (2 + 2 + 2), point 6 CH₃ (3) → 13 H on carbon; plus 1 H in –OH → 14 H. One O atom. Molecular formula C₆H₁₄O (hexan-2-ol).
items.specStatementText: Organic compounds can be represented by different types of formulas. These include empirical, molecular, structural (full and condensed), stereochemical and skeletal.
items.random_wrong: C₄H₁₀O
items.working: Carbon atoms: 5 segments give 5 + 1 = 6 points, each a carbon atom. Hydrogen atoms (4 bonds per carbon): point 1 CH₃ (3), point 2 CH bonded to OH (1), points 3–5 CH₂ (2 + 2 + 2), point 6 CH₃ (3) → 13 H on carbon; plus 1 H in –OH → 14 H. One O atom. Molecular formula C₆H₁₄O (hexan-2-ol).

items.q: Which compound contains an ester group?
items.correct: CH₃COOCH₃
items.misconception: CH₃COOH
items.why: Condensed formulas of acids (–COOH) and esters (–COO–) share the letters COO, and students match letter strings rather than the atom bonded to the second oxygen. Check what is bonded to the singly bonded oxygen: H gives a carboxyl group (carboxylic acid); a carbon atom gives an ester group.
items.specStatementText: Functional groups give characteristic physical and chemical properties to a compound. Organic compounds are divided into classes according to the functional groups present in their molecules.
items.random_wrong: CH₃CH₂OCH₃

items.q: Which statement gives the defining feature of an unsaturated organic compound?
items.correct: Its molecules contain at least one carbon–carbon double or triple bond.
items.misconception: Its molecules have fewer H atoms than the alkane with the same number of C atoms.
items.why: Alkenes are introduced as having the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, so students use the formula as the test for a C=C bond instead of looking at the bonding. Saturation is about bonding: unsaturated compounds contain C=C or C≡C bonds. Cycloalkanes share the formula CₙH₂ₙ with alkenes but have only single bonds, and halogenoalkanes have fewer hydrogen atoms than alkanes but are saturated.
items.specStatementText: Functional groups give characteristic physical and chemical properties to a compound. Organic compounds are divided into classes according to the functional groups present in their molecules.
items.random_wrong: Some of the carbon atoms in its molecules have formed fewer than four bonds.

items.q: Which pair of compounds are successive members of the same homologous series?
items.correct: CH₃COOH and CH₃CH₂COOH
items.misconception: CH₃CH₂CHO and CH₃COCH₂CH₃
items.why: The 'differ by CH₂' rule is the most memorable and most easily checked part of the definition, so students apply it on its own. Successive members must share the same functional group and general formula as well as differing by CH₂. Check the functional group first, then the CH₂ difference.
items.specStatementText: A homologous series is a family of compounds in which successive members differ by a common structural unit, typically CH₂. Each homologous series can be described by a general formula.
items.random_wrong: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl and CH₃CHClCH₃

items.q: Methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol are successive members of the homologous series of alcohols. Which statement about these four compounds is correct?
items.correct: They fit one general formula and have similar chemical properties.
items.misconception: They share a functional group, so they have the same boiling point.
items.why: The phrase 'similar properties' is remembered without the distinction between chemical and physical properties, and 'similar' drifts to 'the same'. The functional group determines the characteristic chemical reactions. Physical properties depend on the size of the molecule as well, and show a trend along the series.
items.specStatementText: A homologous series is a family of compounds in which successive members differ by a common structural unit, typically CH₂. Each homologous series can be described by a general formula.
items.random_wrong: They are structural isomers of each other, as each has one –OH group.

items.q: The boiling points of four successive alcohols are: methanol 65 °C, ethanol 78 °C, propan-1-ol 97 °C and butan-1-ol 118 °C. Which statement explains this trend?
items.correct: London forces grow with chain length; each molecule still has one –OH group.
items.misconception: Longer molecules have more H atoms, so they form more hydrogen bonds.
items.why: The name 'hydrogen bond' suggests that any hydrogen atom takes part, and students do not attach the requirement for H bonded to N, O or F. Hydrogen bonds form only when H is bonded to N, O or F. C–H hydrogen atoms do not form hydrogen bonds. The rise in boiling point along the alcohols is due to increasing London forces.
items.specStatementText: Successive members of a homologous series show a trend in physical properties.
items.random_wrong: Longer molecules contain more covalent bonds to break on boiling.

items.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CHO?
items.correct: 2-methylbutanal
items.misconception: 3-methylbutanal
items.why: Condensed formulas are read from left to right, and many first examples happen to be written with the functional group on the left. Before numbering, find the parent chain and the principal group, then number from the end that gives the lowest locants. Writing the same molecule backwards must give the same name.
items.specStatementText: “IUPAC nomenclature” refers to a set of rules used by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry to apply systematic names to organic and inorganic compounds.
items.random_wrong: 2-methylbutanol

items.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂Cl?
items.correct: 1-chloro-2-methylbutane
items.misconception: 1-chloro-2-ethylpropane
items.why: Students are taught to start from the functional group. In a condensed formula such as CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CHO the bracketed CH₃ is the first carbon reached from the –CHO end, so the chain is traced into the branch and never compared with the other route. Trace every path through the carbon atoms that includes the functional group carbon and choose the longest. An 'ethyl' branch on carbon 2 of a propane chain signals that a longer chain was missed.
items.specStatementText: “IUPAC nomenclature” refers to a set of rules used by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry to apply systematic names to organic and inorganic compounds.
items.random_wrong: 4-chloro-3-methylbutane

items.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂OH?
items.correct: but-3-en-1-ol
items.misconception: but-1-en-4-ol
items.why: Students first number alkenes, where the C=C bond is the only feature, and carry that rule over to molecules that also have a suffix group. The group named as the suffix (-ol, -al, -one, -oic acid) takes precedence for low locants; the C=C bond (-en-) comes next.
items.specStatementText: “IUPAC nomenclature” refers to a set of rules used by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry to apply systematic names to organic and inorganic compounds.
items.random_wrong: but-4-en-1-ol

items.q: Which compound is a tertiary alcohol?
items.correct: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃
items.misconception: CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
items.why: The words primary, secondary and tertiary mean first, second and third, and the locants 1, 2 and 3 appear in the names, so the two ideas are merged. Count the carbon atoms bonded to the carbon that carries –OH (or the halogen): one is primary, two secondary, three tertiary. The locant does not matter.
items.specStatementText: Structural isomers are molecules that have the same molecular formula but different connectivities.
items.random_wrong: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH

items.q: Which statement about the compound (CH₃)₃CNH₂ is correct?
items.correct: It is a primary amine, as its N atom is bonded to one C atom.
items.misconception: It is a tertiary amine, as the C bonded to N carries three CH₃ groups.
items.why: Alcohols and halogenoalkanes are taught first with the 'carbon bearing the group' rule, and students transfer it to amines without noticing that the amine rule looks at the nitrogen. For amines count the carbon atoms bonded directly to N: one (–NH₂) primary, two (–NH–) secondary, three (–N<) tertiary.
items.specStatementText: Structural isomers are molecules that have the same molecular formula but different connectivities.
items.random_wrong: It is a secondary amine, as its N atom is bonded to two H atoms.

items.q: Which compound is a structural isomer of butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH?
items.correct: CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃
items.misconception: CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO
items.why: Students focus on the carbon skeleton and the functional-group atoms, which are prominent in names and drawings, and do not count hydrogen atoms. Write the molecular formula of each compound and compare every element, hydrogen included, before deciding whether they are isomers.
items.specStatementText: Structural isomers are molecules that have the same molecular formula but different connectivities.
items.random_wrong: HOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃

items.q: Which compound can exist as cis and trans isomers?
items.correct: 1,2-dimethylcyclobutane
items.misconception: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene
items.why: Restricted rotation is taught as 'the cause' of cis–trans isomerism, and students treat it as sufficient rather than as one of two required features. Check both carbon atoms of the C=C bond (or the two ring carbons): if either carries two identical groups, swapping sides gives the same molecule and there are no cis–trans isomers.
items.specStatementText: Stereoisomers have the same constitution (atom identities, connectivities and bond multiplicities) but different spatial arrangements of atoms.
items.random_wrong: 1,3-dichloropropane

items.q: Which compound has a chiral carbon atom?
items.correct: butan-2-ol
items.misconception: propan-2-ol
items.why: Standard examples of chiral carbons, such as butan-2-ol, have the functional group on the chiral carbon, and students generalize from the feature they notice (the functional group) rather than checking all four groups. List the four groups on the carbon, written out in full (CH₃, CH₂CH₃, …), and check that all four are different.
items.specStatementText: Stereoisomers have the same constitution (atom identities, connectivities and bond multiplicities) but different spatial arrangements of atoms.
items.random_wrong: but-2-ene

items.q: A sample of 2-chlorobutane, CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃, is a racemic mixture. Which statement about the sample is correct?
items.correct: It contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers of 2-chlorobutane.
items.misconception: It contains equal amounts of the cis and trans isomers of 2-chlorobutane.
items.why: Both are 'stereoisomers' with the same connectivity, and both are introduced through three-dimensional drawings, so students merge the two types. Identify the feature: C=C or ring with two different groups on each carbon gives cis–trans isomers; a carbon with four different groups gives enantiomers. Cis and trans isomers are not mirror images of each other.
items.specStatementText: Stereoisomers have the same constitution (atom identities, connectivities and bond multiplicities) but different spatial arrangements of atoms.
items.random_wrong: Its molecules are achiral, which is why the sample shows no optical activity.

items.q: Which statement about the molecular ion peak in the mass spectrum of an organic compound is correct?
items.correct: Its m/z value gives the relative molecular mass of the compound.
items.misconception: It is the tallest peak, as most molecules reach the detector unbroken.
items.why: The molecular ion is the first thing students are asked to find, and 'most important peak' is equated with 'biggest peak'. Find M⁺ by position (highest m/z of the whole molecule), not by height. For propanone, butanone and ethyl ethanoate, the base peak is at m/z 43, a fragment.
items.specStatementText: Mass spectrometry (MS) of organic compounds can cause fragmentation of molecules.
items.random_wrong: It is due to an ion formed when a molecule gains an electron.

items.q: The mass spectrum of pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ (M_r = 86), has a molecular ion peak at m/z 86 and a peak at m/z 57. Fragment data: m/z 29 = C₂H₅⁺ or CHO⁺; m/z 57 = C₄H₉⁺ or C₂H₅CO⁺. Which species is responsible for the peak at m/z 57?
items.correct: the ion C₂H₅CO⁺, left when C₂H₅ (mass 29) is lost from the molecular ion
items.misconception: the ion C₂H₅⁺, left behind when a fragment of mass 57 is lost
items.why:
Data tables list both 'fragments' and 'mass lost', and students use the two kinds of number interchangeably. Each fragment peak is a positive ion that reached the detector. Subtract its m/z from the M⁺ value to find the mass of the uncharged piece that was lost.

Working: Mass lost from M⁺ = 86 − 57 = 29, which corresponds to C₂H₅ (2 × 12 + 5 × 1 = 29). Detected ion: C₂H₅CO⁺ = 2 × 12 + 5 × 1 + 12 + 16 = 57. The alternative C₄H₉⁺ (4 × 12 + 9 = 57) would need four carbon atoms bonded together without the oxygen, which pentan-3-one does not contain.
items.specStatementText: Mass spectrometry (MS) of organic compounds can cause fragmentation of molecules.
items.random_wrong: an impurity of M_r 57 in the sample, as pure pentan-3-one gives only M⁺
items.working: Mass lost from M⁺ = 86 − 57 = 29, which corresponds to C₂H₅ (2 × 12 + 5 × 1 = 29). Detected ion: C₂H₅CO⁺ = 2 × 12 + 5 × 1 + 12 + 16 = 57. The alternative C₄H₉⁺ (4 × 12 + 9 = 57) would need four carbon atoms bonded together without the oxygen, which pentan-3-one does not contain.

items.q: A compound, C₃H₆O₂, has an IR spectrum with a very broad absorption across 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ and a strong absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹. Characteristic ranges: O–H (alcohols) 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; O–H (carboxylic acids) 2500–3000 cm⁻¹; C–H 2850–3090 cm⁻¹; C=O 1700–1750 cm⁻¹; C=C 1620–1680 cm⁻¹. Which interpretation is correct?
items.correct: It is a carboxylic acid: there is a broad acid O–H band and a C=O band.
items.misconception: It is an alcohol: the broad band is the O–H of a hydroxyl group.
items.why: The alcohol O–H band is the first IR band students learn to recognize, and data tables list two O–H ranges that are easily merged. Read the wavenumber range: 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ for alcohols, 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ (very broad) for carboxylic acids, together with C=O at 1700–1750 cm⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: Infrared (IR) spectra can be used to identify the type of bond present in a molecule.
items.random_wrong: It is an ester: the 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ band is due only to C–H bonds.

items.q: Carbon dioxide and water vapour are greenhouse gases, but nitrogen and oxygen are not. Which statement explains this difference?
items.correct: Vibrations of CO₂ and H₂O change their dipole moment, so they absorb IR.
items.misconception: CO₂ and H₂O are polar molecules, but N₂ and O₂ are non-polar molecules.
items.why: Students learn that IR absorption needs a change in dipole moment and shorten this to 'needs a dipole', i.e. a polar molecule. The requirement is a change in dipole moment during a vibration, not a permanent dipole. N₂ and O₂ have no such vibration; CO₂ and H₂O do.
items.specStatementText: Infrared (IR) spectra can be used to identify the type of bond present in a molecule.
items.random_wrong: Like the ozone layer, CO₂ and H₂O absorb the Sun's ultraviolet radiation.

items.q: Which describes the ¹H NMR spectrum of 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH?
items.correct: two signals, whose areas are in the ratio 9:1
items.misconception: one signal, as only H atoms on carbon give signals
items.why: Many worked examples focus on C–H environments and splitting, and the –OH signal is often a singlet that is treated as unimportant, so students conclude it does not appear. Count every hydrogen environment, including O–H hydrogen atoms, when predicting the number of signals.
items.specStatementText: Proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (¹H NMR) gives information on the different chemical environments of hydrogen atoms in a molecule.
items.random_wrong: two signals, with areas in the ratio 1:1

items.q: A compound, C₂H₄O₂, is either ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, or methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃. Its ¹H NMR spectrum shows two singlets, at δ 2.1 and δ 11.5. Typical chemical shifts: R–COOH 9.0–13.0 ppm; H on a carbon bonded to the singly bonded O of an ester, –C(=O)–O–CH₃, 3.7–4.8 ppm. Which conclusion is correct?
items.correct: Ethanoic acid: δ 11.5 is the COOH proton and δ 2.1 is the CH₃ group.
items.misconception: Methyl methanoate: its two H environments give two singlets.
items.why: Counting signals and reading splitting patterns are rule-based, while chemical shifts require a data table, so students stop once the easier features match. Check each signal's chemical shift against the data table as well as its area and splitting. A structure must fit all three.
items.specStatementText: Proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (¹H NMR) gives information on the different chemical environments of hydrogen atoms in a molecule.
items.random_wrong: Methyl methanoate: an O–H proton gives no signal, so the acid gives one.

items.q: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, which splitting pattern does the signal from the CH₃ group bonded to the carbonyl carbon show?
items.correct: a singlet, as the adjacent carbon has no H atoms
items.misconception: a quartet, as the CH₃ group itself contains three H atoms
items.why: The rule is often memorized as a formula without the word 'neighbouring', and the hydrogen atoms of the group itself are the ones in front of the student. Look at the neighbouring carbon atoms, count their hydrogen atoms, and add one. In CH₃CH₂– the CH₃ signal is a triplet and the CH₂ signal a quartet.
items.specStatementText: Individual signals can be split into clusters of peaks.
items.random_wrong: a doublet, as its carbon is bonded to one other carbon atom

items.q: Compound X, C₄H₈O₂ (M_r = 88), gives these data. IR: sharp absorptions at 2850–3000 cm⁻¹, a strong absorption at 1740 cm⁻¹ and no broad absorption (ranges: C–H 2850–3090 cm⁻¹; C=O 1700–1750 cm⁻¹; O–H in carboxylic acids 2500–3000 cm⁻¹, very broad). MS: M⁺ at m/z 88 and a peak at m/z 29 (CHO⁺ or C₂H₅⁺). ¹H NMR: δ 1.3 (triplet, 3H), δ 2.0 (singlet, 3H), δ 4.1 (quartet, 2H); H on a carbon bonded to the singly bonded O of an ester, –C(=O)–O–CH₂–, appears at 3.7–4.8 ppm. Which identification is consistent with all the data?
items.correct: Ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃: the δ 4.1 quartet is a CH₂ bonded to the ester O and to a CH₃.
items.misconception: Butanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH: the bands at 2850–3000 and 1740 cm⁻¹ are its O–H and C=O.
items.why: The two wavenumber ranges overlap in data tables, and students read only positions, not band shapes. Use the shape of the band as well as its position. A very broad band from 2500 to 3000 cm⁻¹ indicates a carboxylic acid O–H; sharp absorptions just below or above 3000 cm⁻¹ are C–H.
items.specStatementText: Data from different techniques are often combined in structural analysis.
items.random_wrong: Methyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃: its CH₃, CH₂ and OCH₃ give a triplet, quartet and singlet.

items.q: Which compound is a secondary halogenoalkane?
items.correct: CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₂CH₃
items.misconception: CH₃CH₂CH₂CHBr₂
items.why: 'Tertiary' and 'tri-' both suggest three, and diols and triols are named with number prefixes, so students link the class to the number of groups. The class describes one –OH group or halogen atom and its carbon: count the carbon atoms bonded to the carbon that carries it.
items.specStatementText: Structural isomers are molecules that have the same molecular formula but different connectivities.
items.random_wrong: (CH₃)₂CBrCH₂CH₃

items.q: The boiling points of the first five straight-chain alkanes are: methane −162 °C, ethane −89 °C, propane −42 °C, butane −1 °C and pentane 36 °C. Which statement about this trend is correct?
items.correct: The rise per CH₂ unit shrinks along the series, so hexane is expected to boil below 73 °C.
items.misconception: Each further CH₂ unit adds the same rise as the last, 37 °C, so hexane is expected to boil at 73 °C.
items.why:
Students meet 'differ by CH₂' and 'regular trend' together and take 'regular' to mean 'linear'; early members (a 37 °C step from butane to pentane) are the ones quoted most often. Describe the trend as a rise that becomes gradually smaller: the London forces added by one more CH₂ unit make a smaller proportional difference to a longer molecule.

Working: Successive differences: −89 − (−162) = 73 °C; −42 − (−89) = 47 °C; −1 − (−42) = 41 °C; 36 − (−1) = 37 °C. The steps decrease, so the next step is smaller than 37 °C and hexane is expected to boil below 36 + 37 = 73 °C (it boils at 69 °C).
items.specStatementText: Successive members of a homologous series show a trend in physical properties.
items.random_wrong: The rise is caused by hydrogen bonding, which grows as H atoms are added to the chain.
items.working: Successive differences: −89 − (−162) = 73 °C; −42 − (−89) = 47 °C; −1 − (−42) = 41 °C; 36 − (−1) = 37 °C. The steps decrease, so the next step is smaller than 37 °C and hexane is expected to boil below 36 + 37 = 73 °C (it boils at 69 °C).

items.q: In a high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum, one signal is split into a quartet. What does this show about the structure?
items.correct: The carbon atom(s) adjacent to the group carry three hydrogen atoms in total.
items.misconception: The carbon atom giving the signal is bonded to three other carbon atoms in the chain.
items.why: The rule is taught as 'count the neighbours', and students count neighbouring atoms rather than the hydrogen atoms on them. Count hydrogen atoms, not carbon atoms: the H atoms on carbons directly bonded to the carbon carrying the signal's hydrogen atoms.
items.specStatementText: Individual signals can be split into clusters of peaks.
items.random_wrong: The group giving the signal is a CH₃ group, since its three H atoms give 3 + 1 = 4 peaks.

items.q: Compound Y, C₄H₈O (M_r = 72), gives these data. IR: a strong absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹, sharp absorptions at 2850–3000 cm⁻¹ and no absorption between 3100 and 3700 cm⁻¹ (ranges: C=O 1700–1750 cm⁻¹; C–H 2850–3090 cm⁻¹; O–H in alcohols 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; C=C 1620–1680 cm⁻¹). MS: M⁺ at m/z 72, peaks at m/z 57 and m/z 43. ¹H NMR: δ 1.0 (triplet, 3H), δ 2.1 (singlet, 3H), δ 2.4 (quartet, 2H). Which structure is consistent with all the data?
items.correct: Butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃: the δ 2.1 singlet is CH₃CO and the ethyl group gives the triplet and quartet.
items.misconception: Butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO: the strong band at 1715 cm⁻¹ with no O–H band identifies the aldehyde C=O group.
items.why:
Worked examples often begin with a decisive band, and students stop at the first match; examiner reports repeatedly note candidates who name a compound consistent with one spectrum but contradicted by another. Treat each technique as a constraint and check the proposed structure against every datum: a C=O band alone allows aldehyde, ketone, acid, ester and amide.

Working: M_r = 4 × 12 + 8 × 1 + 16 = 72, matching M⁺ at m/z 72. Loss of CH₃ (15) gives 72 − 15 = 57, the C₂H₅CO⁺ ion; loss of C₂H₅ (29) gives 72 − 29 = 43, the CH₃CO⁺ ion. Signal areas 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 hydrogen atoms, matching C₄H₈O.
items.specStatementText: Data from different techniques are often combined in structural analysis.
items.random_wrong: 2-Methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CHCHO: its three hydrogen environments give the three signals observed.
items.working: M_r = 4 × 12 + 8 × 1 + 16 = 72, matching M⁺ at m/z 72. Loss of CH₃ (15) gives 72 − 15 = 57, the C₂H₅CO⁺ ion; loss of C₂H₅ (29) gives 72 − 29 = 43, the CH₃CO⁺ ion. Signal areas 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 hydrogen atoms, matching C₄H₈O.

items.q: The diagram shows the skeletal formula of a hydrocarbon. Which condensed structural formula represents the same compound?
items.correct: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃
items.misconception: CH₃CH₂(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃
items.why: Students learn CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–… as a pattern from unbranched alkanes and apply it mechanically, without checking that each carbon forms exactly four bonds. Work out the hydrogen atoms carbon by carbon: count the bonds drawn to each carbon atom and add hydrogen atoms up to a total of four bonds. A molecular formula with an odd number of H atoms for a compound of C, H and O alone signals an error.
items.specStatementText: Organic compounds can be represented by different types of formulas. These include empirical, molecular, structural (full and condensed), stereochemical and skeletal.
items.random_wrong: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃

items.q: The diagram shows the skeletal formula of a compound. Which statement about its functional groups is correct?
items.correct: It contains amino and ketone groups, since –NH₂ and C=O are on different carbons.
items.misconception: It contains an amido group, since –NH₂ is bonded to a carbon atom.
items.why: The two names differ by one letter and both groups contain nitrogen bonded to hydrogen, so students key on the –NH₂ and ignore whether the carbon it is attached to carries a C=O. Look at the carbon bonded to nitrogen: C=O on that carbon means amido (amide); no C=O means amino (amine).
items.specStatementText: Functional groups give characteristic physical and chemical properties to a compound. Organic compounds are divided into classes according to the functional groups present in their molecules.
items.random_wrong: It contains an ester group, since the C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons.

items.q: The diagram shows the skeletal formulas of four compounds, P, Q, R and S. Which two are successive members of the same homologous series?
items.correct: P and R
items.misconception: Q and R
items.why: Both terms describe families of 'related' organic compounds, and both are introduced in the same lesson with similar-looking lists of formulas. Homologues: same functional group and general formula, formulas differing by CH₂ (CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH). Isomers: identical molecular formula, different structure (propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol).
items.specStatementText: A homologous series is a family of compounds in which successive members differ by a common structural unit, typically CH₂. Each homologous series can be described by a general formula.

items.q: The diagram shows the skeletal formula of a halogenoalkane. What is its IUPAC name?
items.correct: 2-bromo-3-methylhexane
items.misconception: 3-methyl-2-bromohexane
items.why:
Alcohol names such as 2-methylbutan-1-ol put the functional group right against the parent chain with the branches first. Students copy that pattern for halogenoalkanes, where the halogen is named by a prefix instead. In halogenoalkanes the halogen is named by a prefix, just as an alkyl branch is. All prefixes are listed in alphabetical order (chloro before ethyl before methyl), each with its locant.

Working: Longest continuous chain: six carbon atoms, so the parent is hexane. Numbering from the right-hand end puts Br on C2 and CH₃ on C3 (locants 2,3); from the left they would be 5,4. Prefixes in alphabetical order: bromo before methyl. Name: 2-bromo-3-methylhexane.
items.specStatementText: “IUPAC nomenclature” refers to a set of rules used by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry to apply systematic names to organic and inorganic compounds.
items.random_wrong: 2-bromo-3-propylbutane

items.q: The diagram shows the skeletal formula of a compound. What is its IUPAC name?
items.correct: 4-methylpent-3-en-2-ol
items.misconception: 4-methylpent-4-en-2-ol
items.why:
A double bond involves two carbon atoms, and nothing in the formula shows which number to use, so students choose the one they reach last or pick either. Always use the lower of the two numbers of the carbon atoms joined by the C=C bond: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ is but-2-ene, not but-3-ene.

Working: The suffix -ol takes the lowest locant, so number from the right-hand end: OH on C2, C=C between C3 and C4 (locant 3), methyl on C4. Name: 4-methylpent-3-en-2-ol.
items.specStatementText: “IUPAC nomenclature” refers to a set of rules used by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry to apply systematic names to organic and inorganic compounds.
items.random_wrong: 2-methylpent-2-en-4-ol
items.working: The suffix -ol takes the lowest locant, so number from the right-hand end: OH on C2, C=C between C3 and C4 (locant 3), methyl on C4. Name: 4-methylpent-3-en-2-ol.

items.q: The diagram shows four skeletal formulas, P, Q, R and S. Which one represents a structural isomer of butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃?
items.correct: compound S
items.misconception: compound P
items.why: Students compare formulas as strings of symbols or as pictures on the page, not as sets of connected atoms, so a new drawing looks like a new molecule. Isomers have different connectivity. Follow the chain atom by atom: if the sequence of bonded atoms is the same, the two formulas show one compound.
items.specStatementText: Structural isomers are molecules that have the same molecular formula but different connectivities.
items.random_wrong: compound Q

items.q: The diagram shows two skeletal formulas, P and Q, of pent-2-ene. Which statement about P and Q is correct?
items.correct: P and Q are cis–trans isomers, since rotation about the C=C bond is restricted.
items.misconception: P and Q are the same compound, since the chain can rotate freely about the C=C bond.
items.why: Students see single-bond chains drawn in many conformations that are all the same compound, and extend the freedom to double bonds; ball-and-stick models with springs also rotate easily. Model a C=C bond with two connections between the same pair of atoms: it cannot twist. Cis and trans forms are separate compounds with different properties.
items.specStatementText: Stereoisomers have the same constitution (atom identities, connectivities and bond multiplicities) but different spatial arrangements of atoms.
items.random_wrong: P and Q are enantiomers, since each is the non-superimposable mirror image of the other.

items.q: The diagram shows stereochemical formulas of two halogenoalkanes, P and Q. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Only P is chiral, since its central carbon atom carries four different groups.
items.misconception: Both are chiral, since each has a carbon atom bonded to Cl, H and two alkyl groups.
items.why: Standard examples of chiral carbons, such as butan-2-ol, have the functional group on the chiral carbon, and students generalize from the feature they notice (the functional group) rather than checking all four groups. List the four groups on the carbon, written out in full (CH₃, CH₂CH₃, …), and check that all four are different.
items.specStatementText: Stereoisomers have the same constitution (atom identities, connectivities and bond multiplicities) but different spatial arrangements of atoms.
items.random_wrong: Both are chiral, since the mirror image of each, with Cl and H swapped, looks different.

items.q: The diagram shows the mass spectrum of propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. Which statement about the spectrum is correct?
items.correct: The base peak at m/z 31 is CH₂OH⁺, formed when the molecular ion loses C₂H₅.
items.misconception: An uncharged C₂H₅ fragment gives the peak at m/z 29 as CH₂OH⁺ forms.
items.why:
Spectra show many fragment peaks, so students assume every piece of the molecule appears somewhere, without linking detection to charge. A mass spectrometer detects ions only. When M⁺ splits, one fragment keeps the charge and is detected at its m/z; the other is uncharged and invisible.

Working: M_r of propan-1-ol = 3 × 12 + 8 × 1 + 16 = 60, so the molecular ion is at m/z 60. CH₂OH⁺ = 12 + 2 + 16 + 1 = 31, so the base peak at m/z 31 is CH₂OH⁺; the mass lost is 60 − 31 = 29 = C₂H₅ (24 + 5).
items.specStatementText: Mass spectrometry (MS) of organic compounds can cause fragmentation of molecules.
items.random_wrong: The peak at m/z 31 is the molecular ion, since it is the tallest peak.

items.q: The diagram shows the IR spectrum of a compound with molecular formula C₄H₈O₂. Characteristic ranges: O–H (alcohols) 3200–3600 cm⁻¹, broad; O–H (carboxylic acids) 2500–3000 cm⁻¹, very broad; C–H 2850–3090 cm⁻¹; C=O 1700–1750 cm⁻¹; C=C 1620–1680 cm⁻¹; C–O 1050–1410 cm⁻¹. To which class does the compound belong?
items.correct: an ester, as the band at 1740 cm⁻¹ is C=O and there is no O–H band
items.misconception: an unsaturated compound, as the band at 1740 cm⁻¹ is a C=C absorption
items.why:
Students remember that double bonds absorb in the 1600–1750 cm⁻¹ region without learning the separate ranges. Match the band to the table range for each bond: C=O 1700–1750 cm⁻¹; C=C 1620–1680 cm⁻¹.

Working: The band at 1740 cm⁻¹ lies in the C=O range, 1700–1750 cm⁻¹. The narrow band near 2980 cm⁻¹ lies in the C–H range, 2850–3090 cm⁻¹; there is no band at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and no very broad band across 2500–3000 cm⁻¹, so there is no O–H. Bands at 1240 and 1050 cm⁻¹ lie in the C–O range, 1050–1410 cm⁻¹. C=O plus C–O with no O–H: an ester.
items.specStatementText: Infrared (IR) spectra can be used to identify the type of bond present in a molecule.

items.q: The diagram shows the low-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, with the relative area of each signal. Typical chemical shifts: H on a carbon bonded to O, 3.3–4.5 ppm; R–OH, 1.0–6.0 ppm; R–CH₃, 0.9–1.0 ppm. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The signal at δ 3.6, of area 2, is the CH₂ group bonded to the oxygen atom.
items.misconception: The four signals should have equal areas, since each stands for one chemical environment.
items.why:
Students learn that 'one signal per environment' and treat each signal as a count of one. Use the integration trace: the ratio of areas equals the ratio of numbers of hydrogen atoms in the environments, for example 9:1 in (CH₃)₃COH.

Working: Relative areas 3 : 2 : 2 : 1 match CH₃ (3H), CH₂ (2H), CH₂O (2H) and OH (1H). The signal at δ 3.6 lies in the 3.3–4.5 ppm range for H on a carbon bonded to O and has area 2, so it is the –CH₂OH group.
items.specStatementText: Proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (¹H NMR) gives information on the different chemical environments of hydrogen atoms in a molecule.
items.random_wrong: The signal at δ 2.3, of area 1, cannot be the O–H hydrogen, since O–H hydrogens give no signal.

items.q: The diagram shows the high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl. Which statement about the splitting is correct?
items.correct: The signal at δ 3.6 is a quartet because the adjacent CH₃ group carries three H atoms.
items.misconception: The signal at δ 3.6 shows an environment containing four equivalent H atoms.
items.why:
Integration and splitting are both 'counting' ideas met in the same lesson; the peak count is the more visible feature, so students attach the hydrogen count to it. Read area for the number of hydrogen atoms in the group and splitting for the number on the neighbouring carbon atoms: a CH₂ next to CH₃ is a quartet with area 2.

Working: CH₂Cl hydrogens: the neighbouring CH₃ carbon carries n = 3 H atoms, so the signal has n + 1 = 4 lines (quartet). CH₃ hydrogens: the neighbouring CH₂ carbon carries n = 2, so 2 + 1 = 3 lines (triplet).
items.specStatementText: Individual signals can be split into clusters of peaks.
items.random_wrong: The signal at δ 3.6 is the CH₃ group, because three H atoms give 3 + 1 = 4 lines.
items.working: CH₂Cl hydrogens: the neighbouring CH₃ carbon carries n = 3 H atoms, so the signal has n + 1 = 4 lines (quartet). CH₃ hydrogens: the neighbouring CH₂ carbon carries n = 2, so 2 + 1 = 3 lines (triplet).

items.q: Does a formula such as C₃H₈O show the structure of a molecule?
items.correct: No. C₃H₈O is a molecular formula: it shows the number of each type of atom, not which atoms are bonded to which. A structural formula such as CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ shows the connectivity.
items.misconception: A formula that lists every atom in the molecule is a structural formula, because it shows everything the molecule contains.
items.why: The words 'molecular', 'structural' and 'condensed' all describe formulas students see written in one line, and a formula that accounts for every atom seems complete. A structural formula must show connectivity, either with drawn bonds (full) or by listing the groups carbon by carbon (condensed). A molecular formula gives only the numbers of atoms.
items.specStatementText: Organic compounds can be represented by different types of formulas. These include empirical, molecular, structural (full and condensed), stereochemical and skeletal.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a molecular formula identify a single compound?
items.correct: No. Structural isomers share a molecular formula: C₃H₈O is propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol and methoxyethane.
items.misconception: Each molecular formula belongs to one compound only, so knowing the molecular formula identifies the substance.
items.why: In inorganic chemistry a formula such as NaCl or H₂O does identify one substance, and students extend this to organic compounds. Organic molecules with the same atoms can be connected in different ways. A structural (or skeletal) formula is needed to specify which isomer is meant.

items.q: Which points in a skeletal formula represent carbon atoms?
items.correct: Every vertex (bend) and every line end, unless another atom symbol is written there.
items.misconception: Only the bends in the zig-zag are carbon atoms; the ends of the lines are simply where the drawing stops.
items.why: Textbook statements often stress that 'each corner is a carbon atom', and students do not generalize this to the terminal carbons, which do not look like corners. A line end with no symbol is a carbon atom, usually a CH₃ group. Count ends and vertices together to find the number of carbon atoms.

items.q: What is the difference between an ester and an ether?
items.correct: An ester contains –COO–, a carbonyl carbon bonded to an oxygen that is bonded to another carbon (R–COO–R′). An ether contains only an oxygen single-bonded between two carbon atoms, R–O–R′, with no C=O.
items.misconception: Esters and ethers are the same kind of compound, because both have an oxygen atom joining two carbon chains.
items.why: The names are similar, and both groups contain a C–O–C linkage, so students identify the linkage and do not check for the C=O. Look at the carbon next to the linking oxygen: if it is double-bonded to another oxygen (–COO–), the group is an ester; if not (–O–), it is an alkoxy group and the compound is an ether.
items.specStatementText: Functional groups give characteristic physical and chemical properties to a compound. Organic compounds are divided into classes according to the functional groups present in their molecules.

items.q: Does a ketone such as CH₃COCH₂CH₃ contain an ester group?
items.correct: No. A ketone has a carbonyl group, C=O, bonded to two carbon atoms (–CO–). An ester has a second oxygen: –COO– with that oxygen bonded to carbon.
items.misconception: A compound with a C=O group bonded to carbon on both sides of the chain contains an ester group; the second oxygen does not need to be checked.
items.why: Condensed formulas of ketones (–CO–) and esters (–COO–) differ by one letter, and students key on the carbonyl group, the feature both share, without counting the oxygen atoms on that carbon. Count the oxygen atoms on the carbonyl carbon. One oxygen (–CO–) within a chain is a ketone; –COO– with the second oxygen bonded to carbon is an ester.

items.q: In an unsaturated compound such as ethene, does each carbon atom still form four bonds?
items.correct: Yes. Each carbon in CH₂=CH₂ forms two bonds to hydrogen atoms and a double bond (two bonds) to the other carbon: four bonds in total.
items.misconception: In an unsaturated compound some carbon atoms have not formed all four of their bonds; they have a spare, unused bond.
items.why: 'Unsaturated' is read in its everyday sense of 'not full', and the ability of alkenes to add further atoms is pictured as filling empty bonding positions. Every carbon atom in a stable organic molecule forms four bonds. 'Unsaturated' means that the molecule contains a multiple bond between carbon atoms, which can open up to add more atoms.

items.q: Is a halogenoalkane or an alcohol such as CH₃CH₂OH unsaturated?
items.correct: No. CH₃CH₂OH has only single bonds between its carbon atoms, so it is saturated. Having a functional group does not make a compound unsaturated.
items.misconception: Only alkanes are saturated; once an H atom is replaced by a functional group such as –OH or –Cl, the compound becomes unsaturated.
items.why: Saturated and unsaturated are first taught with the pair 'alkanes are saturated, alkenes are unsaturated', and students overgeneralize to 'anything that is not an alkane is unsaturated'. Saturated means only single bonds between carbon atoms; unsaturated means at least one C=C or C≡C. Chloroethane and ethanol are saturated.

items.q: Do ethane, ethene and ethyne form a homologous series?
items.correct: No. They belong to three different homologous series (alkanes, alkenes, alkynes), each with its own functional group and general formula. They differ by H₂, not by CH₂.
items.misconception: Ethane, ethene and ethyne are successive members of one homologous series, because their formulas change by a regular unit (H₂).
items.why: The three are taught together as a sequence of 'hydrocarbons with two carbons', and the regular change of formula looks like the regular change that defines a series. A homologous series keeps the functional group fixed and adds CH₂ units: ethane, propane, butane are homologues; ethene, propene, but-1-ene are homologues.
items.specStatementText: A homologous series is a family of compounds in which successive members differ by a common structural unit, typically CH₂. Each homologous series can be described by a general formula.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do all the alcohols undergo similar reactions?
items.correct: Because they have the same functional group, the –OH group, which is where their characteristic reactions take place.
items.misconception: The chemical reactions of an organic compound depend mainly on the length of its carbon chain, so members of a series with different chain lengths react quite differently.
items.why: Chain length visibly changes physical properties along a series, and students extend the effect of size to chemical behaviour instead of locating reactivity in the functional group. Chemical properties are characteristic of the functional group; chain length has only a minor effect on them. That is why a homologous series can be treated as a family with shared reactions.
items.specStatementText: A homologous series is a family of compounds in which successive members differ by a common structural unit, typically CH₂. Each homologous series can be described by a general formula.

items.q: When an alcohol or alkane boils, which forces are overcome?
items.correct: The intermolecular forces between molecules (London forces and, for alcohols, hydrogen bonds). The covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken.
items.misconception: Boiling breaks covalent bonds within the molecules, so compounds with more covalent bonds have higher boiling points.
items.why: Students think of 'breaking bonds' whenever energy is supplied, and the word 'bond' in 'hydrogen bond' blurs the line between intramolecular and intermolecular forces. Boiling separates whole molecules from each other; the molecules in the vapour are the same molecules as in the liquid. The trend reflects stronger intermolecular forces in larger molecules.
items.specStatementText: Successive members of a homologous series show a trend in physical properties.

items.q: Why do larger molecules in a homologous series have higher boiling points?
items.correct: Because larger molecules have more electrons and a greater surface area of contact, so the London forces between molecules are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them.
items.misconception: Heavier molecules have higher boiling points because of their mass itself: they need more energy simply to move, whatever the forces between them.
items.why: Relative molecular mass is often quoted as the thing that increases along a series, and students take the correlated quantity (mass) as the cause instead of the intermolecular forces. Boiling point is determined by the strength of the intermolecular forces. The number of electrons, and so the strength of London forces, rises with molecular size, which is why mass and boiling point correlate.
items.specStatementText: Successive members of a homologous series show a trend in physical properties.

items.q: What is the difference between the suffixes -ol and -al?
items.correct: -ol means a hydroxyl group (alcohol, –OH); -al means an aldehyde group (–CHO, a carbonyl at the end of the chain).
items.misconception: -ol and -al are two spellings of the same ending for oxygen-containing compounds, and either can be used.
items.why: The suffixes differ by one letter, and both belong to compounds containing C, H and one oxygen atom, so students do not tie each suffix to a specific group. Match the suffix to the functional group: –OH gives -ol (ethanol), –CHO gives -al (ethanal), a ketone –CO– gives -one (propanone).

items.q: When a molecule has both a branch and a functional group, which should receive the lower locant?
items.correct: The functional group named as the suffix. For CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂OH the name is 3-methylbutan-1-ol, not 2-methylbutan-4-ol.
items.misconception: The chain is numbered from the end nearest a branch, so that the alkyl group gets the lowest number.
items.why: Alkane nomenclature, taught first, numbers from the end nearest the branch, and students do not update the rule when a suffix group is introduced. The suffix group has priority for the lowest locant. Branches are numbered according to the direction that the suffix group fixes.
items.specStatementText: “IUPAC nomenclature” refers to a set of rules used by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry to apply systematic names to organic and inorganic compounds.

items.q: Is 2-methylpropan-1-ol, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH, a tertiary alcohol because it contains a carbon bonded to three other carbons?
items.correct: No. It is a primary alcohol: the carbon bearing –OH (the CH₂) is bonded to only one other carbon. The branched carbon does not carry the –OH.
items.misconception: An alcohol is tertiary if its molecule contains a carbon atom bonded to three other carbon atoms anywhere in the chain.
items.why: Tertiary alcohols are usually drawn with a prominent branched carbon, so students look for branching in general rather than at the carbon bonded to the functional group. Classify using only the carbon atom bonded to the –OH group, counting the carbon atoms attached to it.

items.q: Does an amine with two hydrogen atoms on its nitrogen, or a halogenoalkane with two hydrogen atoms on the carbon carrying the halogen, count as secondary?
items.correct: No. An amine with –NH₂ has one carbon on the nitrogen and is primary; a secondary amine has two carbon atoms on the nitrogen (–NH–). A –CH₂Br carbon is bonded to one other carbon, so the halogenoalkane is primary.
items.misconception: The class of an amine, alcohol or halogenoalkane is given by the number of hydrogen atoms on the nitrogen (amines) or on the carbon carrying the –OH or halogen (alcohols, halogenoalkanes): two hydrogen atoms make it secondary.
items.why: Students remember that 'a number of atoms on the key atom' decides the class but count the hydrogen atoms, which are the atoms shown explicitly in –NH₂ and –CH₂Br. Count carbon atoms, not hydrogen atoms: on N for amines, on the carbon carrying –OH or the halogen for alcohols and halogenoalkanes. The number of hydrogen atoms falls as the class rises: –NH₂, –NH–, –N<; –CH₂X, –CHX–, –CX<.

items.q: Can 1,3-dichloropropane, ClCH₂CH₂CH₂Cl, exist as cis and trans isomers?
items.correct: No. Rotation about C–C single bonds is free, so the chlorine atoms can take any relative position; the different arrangements are the same compound.
items.misconception: If two groups can be drawn on the same side or on opposite sides of a carbon chain, the molecule has cis and trans isomers.
items.why: Formulas on paper are static, so a drawing with two groups 'up' looks different from one with a group 'down', and students do not picture rotation about single bonds. Cis–trans isomers need restricted rotation, a C=C bond or a ring. Around single bonds in an open chain, the molecule rotates freely between arrangements.

items.q: Is chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl, chiral because its two ends are different?
items.correct: No. No carbon atom in CH₃CH₂Cl carries four different groups (each carries at least two H atoms), so the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image and is not chiral.
items.misconception: Any molecule that is unsymmetrical, with different groups at its two ends, is chiral.
items.why: In everyday language 'asymmetric' means lopsided, and chirality is often introduced with the word 'asymmetric carbon', so students look for overall lopsidedness. Chirality needs non-superimposable mirror images; at IB level, look for a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups.

items.q: Why does a racemic mixture not rotate plane-polarized light?
items.correct: Because it contains equal amounts of two enantiomers that rotate the plane by equal angles in opposite directions, so their effects cancel. Each molecule in the mixture is chiral.
items.misconception: A racemic mixture is optically inactive because its molecules are not chiral.
items.why: Students learn 'chiral compounds are optically active' and reverse it to 'optically inactive samples contain achiral molecules'. Optical inactivity of a sample can arise from cancellation. A racemic mixture is 50:50 in the two enantiomers; separating them gives two optically active samples.

items.q: Do the two enantiomers of a compound have different boiling points?
items.correct: No. Enantiomers have identical physical properties, such as boiling point and density, except for the direction in which they rotate plane-polarized light. They also react identically except in chiral environments.
items.misconception: Enantiomers are different compounds, so they have different physical properties such as boiling points, and can be separated by distillation.
items.why: Structural isomers do have different physical properties, and students extend this to stereoisomers without appreciating that mirror images have identical intermolecular forces. Mirror-image molecules interact identically with non-chiral surroundings. They differ only in their effect on plane-polarized light and in chiral environments, such as enzyme active sites.

items.q: How is the molecular ion formed?
items.correct: By the loss of one electron from the molecule, giving a positive ion, M⁺.
items.misconception: The molecular ion forms when a molecule gains an electron from the electron beam, giving a negative ion, M⁻.
items.why: The ionization step 'bombards' molecules with electrons, and students picture the electrons being added rather than knocking an electron out. A high-energy electron hitting a molecule removes an electron from it: M + e⁻ → M⁺ + 2e⁻. The positive ions are accelerated and detected.

items.q: Do peaks at lower m/z than the molecular ion show that the sample is impure?
items.correct: No. They are fragment ions formed when molecular ions of the pure compound break apart, and they give information about its structure.
items.misconception: A pure compound gives a single peak at its molecular mass; any other peaks come from impurities.
items.why: Students first meet mass spectra of elements, where each peak is a different species (isotope), and carry over 'one peak per substance'. Molecular ions have excess energy and break into fragments. The pattern of fragment peaks is characteristic of the compound's structure.
items.specStatementText: Mass spectrometry (MS) of organic compounds can cause fragmentation of molecules.

items.q: Can a peak at m/z 43 correspond to more than one fragment ion?
items.correct: Yes. Different ions can have the same m/z, for example CH₃CO⁺ and C₃H₇⁺ both have m/z 43. The structure of the compound decides which is possible.
items.misconception: Each m/z value corresponds to one particular fragment, so the first fragment listed for that m/z in a data table identifies the structure.
items.why: Data tables list fragments line by line against m/z values, which looks like a one-to-one key. Use the formula and other data to decide which candidate ion the molecule can form. A propanone molecule, CH₃COCH₃, for instance, has no C₃H₇ unit, so its peak at m/z 43 must be CH₃CO⁺.

items.q: Is the greenhouse effect caused by gases absorbing the Sun's ultraviolet radiation?
items.correct: No. Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface. Absorption of ultraviolet radiation by ozone is a separate process.
items.misconception: Greenhouse gases work like the ozone layer: they absorb ultraviolet radiation coming from the Sun.
items.why: The greenhouse effect and ozone depletion are both taught as atmospheric environmental problems and are frequently conflated in everyday discussion. Sunlight warms the surface, the surface emits infrared radiation, and greenhouse gases absorb that infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, warming the lower atmosphere.

items.q: Do greenhouse gases reflect infrared radiation back to the Earth?
items.correct: No. They absorb infrared radiation, which makes their bonds vibrate, and then re-emit infrared radiation in all directions, some of it back towards the surface.
items.misconception: Greenhouse gases act like a mirror or a pane of glass, reflecting infrared radiation back towards the Earth.
items.why: The 'greenhouse' analogy and diagrams with arrows bouncing off a layer suggest reflection. The process is absorption followed by re-emission, which depends on vibrations that change the dipole moment of the molecule.

items.q: Does each hydrogen atom in a molecule give its own ¹H NMR signal?
items.correct: No. Each distinct chemical environment gives one signal. All hydrogen atoms in the same environment contribute to one signal, whose area reflects how many there are.
items.misconception: The number of signals equals the number of hydrogen atoms in the molecule.
items.why: Students know that ¹H NMR detects hydrogen nuclei and assume each nucleus appears separately, as each atom appears in a formula. Group the hydrogen atoms into sets related by the molecule's symmetry; each set gives one signal.

items.q: Does the chemical shift of a signal depend on how many hydrogen atoms produce it?
items.correct: No. The chemical shift depends on the chemical environment (for example, electronegative atoms nearby shift signals to higher δ). The number of hydrogen atoms is shown by the area under the signal.
items.misconception: Signals from groups with more hydrogen atoms appear at larger chemical shifts.
items.why: Students confuse the two numerical features of a signal, its position (δ) and its size (integration), because both are read from the same spectrum. Read position and area separately: δ identifies the type of environment, the integration gives the number of hydrogen atoms in it.

items.q: Is the CH₃ signal in CH₃COCH₂CH₃ split by the CH₂ hydrogen atoms on the other side of the C=O group?
items.correct: No. At this level splitting is caused by hydrogen atoms on adjacent carbon atoms only. The CH₃ group is bonded to the carbonyl carbon, which carries no hydrogen, so its signal is a singlet.
items.misconception: A signal is split by the nearest hydrogen atoms in the molecule, even when they are on a carbon atom further away across another atom.
items.why: Students look for the closest hydrogen atoms in the formula as written and do not check whether the carbon between them carries hydrogen. Look only at the carbon atoms directly bonded to the carbon that carries the hydrogen atoms producing the signal. If they carry no hydrogen atoms, the signal is a singlet.
items.specStatementText: Individual signals can be split into clusters of peaks.

items.q: Is the end of a short branch line in a skeletal formula a carbon atom?
items.correct: Yes. Every line end with no symbol is a carbon atom, however short the line, so a short stub from the chain is a CH₃ branch.
items.misconception: A short stub drawn off the chain is just a mark, not a carbon atom, so the branch can be ignored and only the zig-zag chain is counted.
items.why: Students learn that line ends are carbon atoms from the ends of the main chain, but a short stub looks like decoration or a bond to a hydrogen atom, so they do not apply the same rule to it. Apply one rule to every line: each end and each vertex is a carbon atom unless another symbol is written there. A short line off the chain is a methyl branch, and the carbon it joins has one fewer H atom.
